splits.legalQuestion: Whether a multiemployer pension plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability after the statutory measurement date (the end of the prior plan year), or whether all such assumptions must be fixed by that date.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether ERISA requires actuarial assumptions used to calculate withdrawal liability to be locked in by the end of the prior plan year. This affects billions of dollars in potential obligations for thousands of employers participating in multiemployer pension plans, as the timing of assumption selection directly controls how much withdrawing employers must pay.

positions.label: Assumptions must be fixed by measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that all actuarial assumptions for calculating withdrawal liability must be selected by the statutory measurement date (end of prior plan year), providing employers greater predictability.

positions.label: Assumptions may be selected after measurement date
positions.summary: Holds that a plan actuary may select actuarial assumptions after the statutory measurement date, allowing the use of more current data in calculating withdrawal liability.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: M & K Employee Solutions v. Trustees of the IAM National Pension Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the term of supervised release is tolled (paused) when a supervisee absconds from supervision, thereby extending the period during which the person can be found to have violated the conditions of supervised release.
splits.description: Circuits split on whether federal courts may apply a judicially-created 'fugitive tolling' doctrine to supervised release, effectively extending court-ordered conditions beyond the time specified in the judgment when a person absconds. The outcome affects sentencing calculations at revocation hearings for thousands of individuals who abscond from supervised release each year.

positions.label: Tolling applies
positions.summary: Holds that the term of supervised release is tolled when a supervisee absconds, allowing courts to extend the period of supervision and find violations beyond the original term.

positions.label: Tolling does not apply
positions.summary: Holds that there is no statutory authority for tolling supervised release when a supervisee absconds, and the term expires as set in the judgment.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2244(b)(1)'s bar on relitigating previously raised claims in habeas proceedings applies to federal prisoners filing motions under Section 2255.
splits.description: Circuits are split 6-to-3 on whether federal prisoners face the categorical bar of § 2244(b)(1) — which prohibits relitigating previously presented claims — in addition to the separate gatekeeping requirements of § 2255(h). If (b)(1) applies, federal prisoners are categorically barred from raising any claim they previously presented; if not, they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s requirements of newly discovered evidence or a new constitutional rule.

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) applies to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that the § 2244(b)(1) bar on relitigating previously raised claims applies to federal prisoners' successive § 2255 motions, imposing an additional gatekeeping requirement beyond § 2255(h).

positions.label: Section 2244(b)(1) does not apply to § 2255 motions
positions.summary: Holds that § 2244(b)(1)'s bar does not apply to federal prisoners' § 2255 motions, meaning they need only satisfy § 2255(h)'s own gatekeeping requirements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a candidate for federal office has Article III standing to challenge a state law that allows the counting of mail-in ballots received after Election Day.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether candidates have standing to bring pre-election challenges to voting procedures. The split implicates whether candidates can show a cognizable injury from election rules before an election occurs, with broad implications for challenges to mail-in voting, ballot counting deadlines, and other election administration practices nationwide.

positions.label: Candidates have standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates have Article III standing to challenge election rules pre-election based on competitive injury or vote-dilution theories.

positions.label: Candidates lack standing
positions.summary: Holds that candidates cannot demonstrate a sufficiently concrete and particularized injury to establish Article III standing for pre-election challenges to ballot-counting rules.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Bost v. Illinois State Board of Elections

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the rule of lenity trumps agency or Sentencing Commission deference (Auer/Kisor deference) when interpreting ambiguous provisions in criminal sentencing guidelines.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether courts should defer to the Sentencing Commission's interpretation of ambiguous Guidelines provisions or instead apply the rule of lenity in favor of the defendant. This split has deepened after the Supreme Court's decisions in Kisor v. Wilkie and Loper Bright Enterprises v. Raimondo, which cast doubt on strong deference regimes.

positions.label: Lenity trumps deference
positions.summary: Holds that the rule of lenity should prevail over agency or Sentencing Commission deference when interpreting ambiguous criminal provisions, preventing agencies from expanding criminal liability through delegated interpretive power.

positions.label: Deference trumps lenity
positions.summary: Holds that agency or Sentencing Commission deference takes precedence over the rule of lenity, allowing deference to anti-defendant interpretations of ambiguous Guidelines provisions.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the word 'and' in the First Step Act's safety-valve provision, 18 U.S.C. § 3553(f)(1), is conjunctive (requiring all three criminal-history criteria to be met for disqualification) or disjunctive (any one criterion is disqualifying).
splits.description: A deep circuit split exists on whether defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria listed in § 3553(f)(1), or whether possessing any one criterion is disqualifying. The split affects whether district courts must impose sentences without regard to statutory minimums and creates disparate sentencing outcomes based on geography.

positions.label: 'And' is conjunctive — all three criteria required
positions.summary: Holds that defendants are disqualified from safety-valve relief only if they meet all three criminal-history criteria, reading 'and' in its ordinary conjunctive sense.

positions.label: 'And' is disjunctive — any one criterion disqualifies
positions.summary: Holds that possessing any one of the three criminal-history criteria is sufficient to disqualify a defendant from safety-valve relief, reading 'and' as 'or' in context.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Sentencing Guidelines' Application Note 1 to § 4B1.2, which includes inchoate offenses like conspiracy in the definition of 'controlled substance offense,' is a valid authoritative interpretation entitled to deference under Stinson and Kisor.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether Application Note 1 to U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2, which expands the definition of 'controlled substance offense' to include conspiracy, aiding and abetting, and attempt, is entitled to controlling deference. Some circuits defer to the commentary as the Commission's authoritative interpretation, while others have held the guideline text is unambiguous and does not include inchoate offenses.

positions.label: Commentary is valid and entitled to deference
positions.summary: Holds that Application Note 1 reasonably interprets an ambiguous guideline and is entitled to controlling weight, so inchoate offenses qualify as 'controlled substance offenses' for career-offender purposes.

positions.label: Commentary exceeds guideline text; inchoate offenses excluded
positions.summary: Holds that the guideline text unambiguously excludes inchoate offenses, and Application Note 1 impermissibly expands the definition beyond the text, so it is not entitled to deference.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a state drug conviction qualifies as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Sentencing Guidelines when the state schedule includes substances not listed on the federal Controlled Substances Act schedules.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether the career-offender guideline's definition of 'controlled substance offense' requires the substance at issue to be federally controlled, or whether any state-controlled substance suffices. The Eighth Circuit holds there is no federal-law limitation, while other circuits require the substance to be federally scheduled.

positions.label: No federal-law limitation — state schedules suffice
positions.summary: Holds that U.S.S.G. § 4B1.2(b) broadly defines 'controlled substance offense' to include offenses under state law, even if the particular substance is not controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act.

positions.label: Federal scheduling required
positions.summary: Holds that the substance underlying a state conviction must be controlled under the federal Controlled Substances Act for the conviction to qualify as a 'controlled substance offense' under the Guidelines.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a non-retroactive change in sentencing law (such as the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment to 18 U.S.C. § 924(c)) can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reason' for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether non-retroactive changes in law can support a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release. Some circuits categorically bar consideration of such changes, while others allow them to be considered alone or in combination with other factors. The Sentencing Commission's 2024 amendment to U.S.S.G. § 1B1.13(b)(6) attempted to resolve this issue, but some circuits have held the amendment exceeds the Commission's statutory authority.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes cannot be considered
positions.summary: Holds that a non-retroactive change in law, whether alone or combined with other factors, cannot contribute to a finding of extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

positions.label: Non-retroactive changes may be considered
positions.summary: Holds that non-retroactive changes in law, including the First Step Act's anti-stacking amendment, may be considered as part of the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a federal prisoner challenging conditions of confinement or BOP decisions regarding the execution of a sentence (such as First Step Act earned time credits) must proceed via habeas corpus or may bring a civil rights action.
splits.description: Circuits have been split for decades on whether habeas corpus is the exclusive remedy for federal prisoners challenging conditions related to the execution of their sentence, or whether civil rights actions (e.g., Bivens or mandamus) are also available. The split is particularly acute in the context of BOP decisions on First Step Act earned time credits and prerelease custody transfers.

positions.label: Habeas is the exclusive remedy
positions.summary: Holds that challenges to the fact, duration, or execution of confinement must be brought through habeas corpus, not through civil rights actions.

positions.label: Civil rights actions also available
positions.summary: Holds that prisoners may bring civil rights or other non-habeas actions to challenge conditions of confinement, even when the challenge relates to the execution of a sentence, so long as the prisoner does not seek release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether district courts may expressly impose sentences upon revocation of supervised release to punish a defendant for the conduct underlying the violation, or whether revocation sentences must be based solely on the breach of the court's trust.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether supervised release revocation sentences may be based on punishing the defendant's underlying violation conduct. The Sixth Circuit allows courts to expressly punish for violations, placing it at the extreme of a circuit split, while other circuits hold that revocation sanctions should focus on the breach of the court's trust rather than punishment for the new conduct.

positions.label: Punishment for violation conduct permitted
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may expressly impose revocation sentences to punish defendants for the conduct that violated conditions of supervised release.

positions.label: Revocation sentences must focus on breach of trust
positions.summary: Holds that revocation sentences should be based on the breach of the court's trust, not on punishing the defendant for the underlying violation conduct.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the appeal deadline for a Hyde Amendment order (attorney's fees in criminal cases) is governed by the civil appeal timeline (60 days when the government is a party) or the criminal appeal timeline (14 days).
splits.description: Circuits split on whether a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case (triggering a 60-day appeal deadline) or part of the criminal case (triggering a 14-day deadline). The Seventh Circuit joined the majority view that the civil deadline applies, but noted the existence of a lopsided circuit split.

positions.label: Civil deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion for attorney's fees is a civil matter ancillary to the criminal case, so the civil appeal deadline (60 days when the government is a party) governs.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: United States v. Manchester Farming Partnership

positions.label: Criminal deadline applies
positions.summary: Holds that a Hyde Amendment motion is part of the criminal case, so the 14-day criminal appeal deadline applies.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether post-petition, pre-conversion increases in the equity of an asset belong to the bankruptcy estate or to debtors who convert from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7 in good faith under 11 U.S.C. § 348(f)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether appreciation in property value that occurs between the filing of a Chapter 13 petition and conversion to Chapter 7 inures to the bankruptcy estate or remains with the debtor. The Ninth Circuit held that such appreciation belongs to the estate, creating a split with circuits that have interpreted § 348(f)(1)(A) to protect debtors' post-petition equity gains upon good-faith conversion.

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the estate
positions.summary: Holds that post-petition, pre-conversion increases in equity belong to the bankruptcy estate upon conversion from Chapter 13 to Chapter 7, based on the broad scope of § 541(a).

positions.label: Appreciation belongs to the debtor
positions.summary: Holds that § 348(f)(1)(A) protects good-faith converting debtors by limiting the estate to the property's value as of the original petition date, with post-petition appreciation remaining with the debtor.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether an order denying a motion to seal documents containing medical information is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine as a matter involving a value of 'high order.'
splits.description: The D.C. Circuit held that an order denying a motion to seal medical records is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because medical privacy is a value of 'high order.' This creates potential tension with other circuits that have taken narrower views of what qualifies for immediate appellate review under the collateral order doctrine.

positions.label: Immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that denial of a motion to seal medical records is immediately appealable under the collateral order doctrine because maintaining privacy in medical treatments and diagnoses is a value of high order that cannot be adequately vindicated by post-judgment review.

positions.label: Not immediately appealable
positions.summary: Holds that orders denying motions to seal generally do not satisfy the collateral order doctrine's requirements because privacy interests can be vindicated on appeal from final judgment.

splits.legalQuestion: What legal standards govern claims of discrimination or unfair treatment in the operation of hospitality or business establishments under Title II of the Civil Rights Act?
splits.description: The circuits disagree on the standards for evaluating discrimination claims in hospitality and business settings, including questions about liability, available remedies, and burdens of proof. The Supreme Court's grant of certiorari indicates the Second Circuit's approach was sufficiently unsettled to warrant review, suggesting a circuit split on these standards.

positions.label: Narrower standards / limited remedies
positions.summary: Holds that claims of discrimination in places of public accommodation are subject to narrower standards of proof or more limited remedies.

positions.label: Broader standards / expanded remedies
positions.summary: Holds that claims of discrimination in places of public accommodation should be evaluated under broader standards with more robust remedies available to plaintiffs.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether state laws categorically barring transgender women from women's sports teams violate the Equal Protection Clause, and what level of scrutiny applies to such classifications.
splits.description: Circuits are beginning to divide on the constitutionality of state laws that categorically prohibit transgender athletes from competing on teams consistent with their gender identity. This split implicates the level of scrutiny applicable to sex-based and transgender classifications and whether as-applied challenges are viable under intermediate scrutiny.

positions.label: Laws likely violate Equal Protection
positions.summary: Holds that categorical bans on transgender women in women's sports likely violate the Equal Protection Clause as applied to transgender individuals who have medically mitigated their sex-based biological advantages.

positions.label: Laws are constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that such laws are a permissible exercise of state authority to maintain fair competition in women's sports based on biological sex differences.

circuits.name: Fourth Circuit
circuits.caseName: B.P.J. v. West Virginia State Board of Education

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Religious Land Use and Institutionalized Persons Act (RLUIPA) clearly authorizes individual-capacity damages suits against state prison officials, and whether Congress has the constitutional power under the Spending Clause to impose such personal liability.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether RLUIPA's text provides sufficiently clear notice to authorize damages claims against prison officials in their individual capacities, implicating Spending Clause limits on Congress's ability to impose personal liability on individuals who are not direct recipients of federal funds.

positions.label: RLUIPA authorizes individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA's text and structure provide clear authorization for damages suits against state prison officials in their individual capacities.

positions.label: RLUIPA does not authorize individual-capacity damages
positions.summary: Holds that RLUIPA does not clearly authorize individual-capacity damages suits against prison officials, and the Spending Clause limits Congress's ability to impose such liability on non-recipients of federal funds.

circuits.name: Fifth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Sossamon v. Lone Star State of Texas

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Landor v. Louisiana Department of Corrections and Public Safety

splits.legalQuestion: Whether a district court may consider factors related to potential errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as part of the 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' analysis for compassionate release under 18 U.S.C. § 3582(c)(1)(A).
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether compassionate release motions may be used to raise claims that overlap with habeas corpus challenges, such as alleged sentencing errors or constitutional violations in the underlying conviction. Some circuits permit consideration of such factors, while others hold that § 3582(c)(1)(A) cannot be used as a substitute for § 2255 habeas relief.

positions.label: May consider conviction/sentence errors
positions.summary: Holds that district courts may consider legal errors or unfairness in a defendant's conviction or sentence as one factor in the extraordinary and compelling reasons analysis for compassionate release.

positions.label: Cannot use compassionate release for habeas-type claims
positions.summary: Holds that § 3582(c)(1)(A) is not an alternative avenue for claims properly raised under § 2255, and errors in conviction or sentencing cannot constitute extraordinary and compelling reasons for compassionate release.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Aviation Administration Authorization Act of 1994 (FAAAA) preempts state-law negligence claims against freight brokers who arrange transportation of property by motor carriers.
splits.description: Circuits are split on whether the FAAAA's broad preemption clause, which prohibits states from enacting laws 'related to a price, route, or service of any... broker,' preempts common-law negligence claims against freight brokers for injuries arising from the carrier's operations. This split affects the liability exposure of freight brokers nationwide.

positions.label: FAAAA preempts broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are preempted by the FAAAA because they relate to the broker's services in arranging transportation.

circuits.name: Ninth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Miller v. C.H. Robinson Worldwide, Inc.

positions.label: FAAAA does not preempt broker negligence claims
positions.summary: Holds that state-law negligence claims against freight brokers are not preempted by the FAAAA because they are generally applicable common-law duties rather than regulations targeting broker services.

circuits.name: Eleventh Circuit
circuits.caseName: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Montgomery v. Caribe Transport II, LLC

splits.legalQuestion: Whether the Federal Insecticide, Fungicide, and Rodenticide Act (FIFRA) preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims based on allegedly inadequate product labeling when the EPA has not required the specific warning.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether FIFRA's preemption provision bars state-law failure-to-warn claims against pesticide manufacturers when the claim is based on the absence of a warning that the EPA did not require. The split affects product liability litigation involving agricultural chemicals and consumer pesticide products.

positions.label: FIFRA preempts failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA preempts state-law failure-to-warn claims that would effectively require labeling different from or in addition to what FIFRA and EPA regulations permit.

positions.label: FIFRA does not preempt failure-to-warn claims
positions.summary: Holds that FIFRA does not preempt state-law failure-to-warn claims because such claims impose requirements 'parallel to' rather than 'in addition to' FIFRA's labeling requirements.

circuits.name: Third Circuit
circuits.caseName: DeKalb Genetics Corp. v. Bayer CropScience

splits.relatedScotusTitle: Monsanto Company v. John L. Durnell

splits.legalQuestion: Whether 18 U.S.C. § 922(g)(3), which prohibits unlawful users of controlled substances from possessing firearms, violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users.
splits.description: Following the Supreme Court's decision in Bruen, circuits have split on whether § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by users of controlled substances — particularly marijuana — is constitutional. Some circuits have upheld the law under historical tradition analysis, while others have found it unconstitutional as applied to marijuana users.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is constitutional
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3)'s prohibition on firearm possession by unlawful drug users is consistent with the nation's historical tradition of firearm regulation and survives Second Amendment scrutiny.

positions.label: Section 922(g)(3) is unconstitutional as applied
positions.summary: Holds that § 922(g)(3) violates the Second Amendment as applied to marijuana users because the government has not demonstrated a historical tradition of disarming persons who use intoxicating substances.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether workers who distribute baked goods to retail stores qualify as 'transportation workers engaged in foreign or interstate commerce' under Section 1 of the Federal Arbitration Act, thereby exempting them from mandatory arbitration agreements.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on the scope of the FAA's Section 1 transportation worker exemption, specifically whether workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of a broader interstate distribution chain are 'transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce.' The split affects the enforceability of arbitration agreements for a broad class of last-mile delivery workers.

positions.label: Broad interpretation — last-mile workers exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who distribute goods to retail stores as part of an interstate distribution chain are transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce exempt from the FAA.

positions.label: Narrow interpretation — last-mile workers not exempt
positions.summary: Holds that workers who merely distribute goods locally to retail stores are not transportation workers engaged in interstate commerce and remain subject to FAA arbitration agreements.

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 47(b) of the Investment Company Act creates a private right of action allowing parties to a contract that violates the ICA to sue in federal court for rescission of that contract.
splits.description: Circuits disagree on whether § 47(b) of the ICA provides an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts made in violation of the Act. This affects the ability of private parties to enforce the ICA's protections against abusive investment company practices through direct federal court actions.

positions.label: Section 47(b) creates a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) creates an implied private right of action for rescission of contracts that violate the Investment Company Act, allowing private parties to sue directly.

circuits.name: Second Circuit
circuits.caseName: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

positions.label: Section 47(b) does not create a private right of action
positions.summary: Holds that § 47(b) is a voidability provision rather than a private right of action, and only the SEC can enforce the ICA's prohibitions.

splits.relatedScotusTitle: FS Credit Opportunities Corp. v. Saba Capital Master Fund

splits.legalQuestion: Whether Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act, as construed under the Gingles framework, can constitutionally compel race-based redistricting as a remedy for vote dilution, and whether compliance with Section 2 constitutes a compelling governmental interest justifying the use of race in drawing district lines.
splits.description: This case raises the question of whether race-conscious redistricting mandated by Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act is constitutionally permissible under the Equal Protection Clause. Lower courts have applied the Gingles framework to require consideration of race, but the constitutionality of this framework as applied is increasingly contested.

positions.label: Section 2 compels constitutionally permissible race-conscious redistricting
positions.summary: Holds that compliance with Section 2 of the VRA, as interpreted under the Gingles framework, constitutes a compelling interest that justifies the use of race in drawing district lines.

positions.label: Section 2's compelled race-based redistricting raises constitutional concerns
positions.summary: Holds or suggests that the Gingles framework's requirement of race-based redistricting may exceed constitutional limits under the Equal Protection Clause, particularly after Dobbs-era equal protection jurisprudence.

circuits.name: Eighth Circuit
circuits.caseName: Arkansas State Conference of the NAACP v. Arkansas Board of Apportionment
